value_source: AEDC Data Dictionary v7.0 (Australian Government Department of Education, February 2025), entry A1
variable_description: How much school the child had missed since the start of the school year, banded, as the teacher reported it on the AvEDI. The dictionary defines the item as a "Variable to indicate how many days the child has been absent from school since the beginning of the school year", asked as "How many days has this child been absent since the start of the year". A1A to A1D on the same row split that absence by reason but are yes-or-no flags, not a decomposition of the band. A1 is not one of the items the dictionary allocates to the physical health and wellbeing domain, so it never enters the PHYS score.
value_definition: A single-digit integer in four bands: 1 for 0 to 1 day, 2 for 2 to 5 days, 3 for 6 to 10 days, 4 for greater than 10 days. The entry publishes no missing-data codes, and its one-character field format leaves no room for the 88 and 99 conventions the dictionary applies to the wider AvEDI item set.
limitation: It cannot give a day count, and its lowest band merges a child who never missed a day with one who missed a single day; A1Z, present only from the 2018 cycle, is the item that separates them. Absence is also counted up to the day the teacher completed the instrument rather than over a full school year, so a child assessed in May and a child assessed in November are not on the same denominator.
rationale: The AEDC Data Dictionary carries a full entry for A1 with the data element description, the instrument wording and the four-band code frame, and its section 7.1 table lists the items allocated to each domain, which excludes A1.
evidence_quote: Variable to indicate how many days the child has been absent from school since the beginning of the school year.
supersedes_rationale: The entry carried only the custodian's wording 'Days absent since the start of the year' with the generic sentence 'The source metadata does not publish a finite value list.' printed as both value definition and limitation, so a reader could not tell that the field is banded or that it does not feed a domain score.

value_domain: AvEDI absence-reason flag (zero days against one or more)
value_source: AEDC Data Dictionary v7.0 (Australian Government Department of Education, February 2025), entry A1a
variable_description: Whether any of the child's absence this school year was for family or cultural reasons, in the teacher's judgement. The dictionary's purpose statement is "To identify, to the best of the teacher's knowledge, how many days the child was absent due to family/cultural obligations, including ceremonies and funerals", and the instrument asks for an approximate number of days. It is one of four reason items, with A1B for illness or injury, A1C for other explained reasons and A1D for unexplained reasons, all sitting beside the total band in A1.
value_definition: A single-digit integer reduced to two states, 0 for zero days and 1 for one or more days, so the day count the teacher supplied is not retained. The 2012 cycle revised the item wording; the dictionary records the end of null values against A1B rather than against this item.
limitation: It carries no volume, so a child absent once for a funeral and a child absent for a fortnight of ceremonies are the same value, and the four reason flags cannot be added up to reproduce the band in A1. The reason is also the teacher's attribution rather than the family's, so an absence the school never had explained to it lands in A1D instead.
rationale: The dictionary's A1a entry gives the item wording, the purpose, the two-value code frame and the 2012 revision history, which is what distinguishes it from a day count.
evidence_quote: A variable to identify how many days the child has been absent from school due to family/cultural obligations.
supersedes_rationale: The entry said only 'Family or cultural obligations' and repeated the generic no-value-list sentence twice, hiding the fact that the published day count is collapsed to a yes-or-no flag.

value_domain: AvEDI absence-reason flag (zero days against one or more)
value_source: AEDC Data Dictionary v7.0 (Australian Government Department of Education, February 2025), entry A1b
variable_description: Whether any of the child's absence this school year was put down to illness or injury. The dictionary describes it as "A variable to identify how many days the child has been absent from school due to illness / injury", asked of the teacher as an approximate number of days and published as a flag. It sits with A1A, A1C and A1D as the four reason splits of the total absence band in A1, and it is the only one of the four that speaks to the child's health.
value_definition: A single-digit integer, 0 for zero days and 1 for one or more days. The dictionary records that the item was renamed from A2a in 2012 and that null values were no longer allowed from that cycle.
limitation: It is not a morbidity measure: it registers absence the school attributed to sickness, so a chronically ill child kept in class and a child kept home for one cold both resolve to 1. It also has nothing to say about the illness itself, which the D-series special needs and diagnosis items in the AEDC special needs table carry instead.
rationale: The dictionary's A1b entry gives the data element description, the instrument wording, the two-value code frame and the 2012 rename from A2a.
evidence_quote: A variable to identify how many days the child has been absent from school due to illness / injury.
supersedes_rationale: The entry carried the custodian's 'Illness or injury' with the generic no-value-list sentence as both definition and limitation, and gave no indication that the underlying day count is not published.

value_domain: AvEDI absence-reason flag (zero days against one or more)
value_source: AEDC Data Dictionary v7.0 (Australian Government Department of Education, February 2025), entry A1c
variable_description: Whether any of the child's absence this school year had a reason the school knew about that was neither health nor family or cultural obligation. The 2009 wording the dictionary reproduces gives the examples "Climatic conditions, financial", which is the clearest guide to what the residual category holds. It is the third of the four reason flags, and the pair to watch is A1C against A1D: the same absence is explained in one and unexplained in the other depending only on whether the family told the school.
value_definition: A single-digit integer, 0 for zero days and 1 for one or more days. The dictionary records that the item was renamed from A3a in 2012 and that the 2009 wording listed climatic and financial reasons as examples.
limitation: It is defined by what the other three flags are not, so its meaning shifts with local practice, and a school that codes weather closures here while another codes them as unexplained will differ for reasons that have nothing to do with the child. It also cannot be read as a hardship indicator, because the 2009 examples name financial reasons only as one instance among several.
rationale: The dictionary's A1c entry publishes the item wording, the code frame and the 2009 revision text that names the intended examples for the residual category.
evidence_quote: A variable to identify how many days the child has been absent from school due to other explained reasons.
supersedes_rationale: The entry said 'Other explained reasons' and repeated the generic no-value-list sentence twice, never saying what the residual category was meant to capture.

value_domain: AvEDI absence-reason flag (zero days against one or more)
value_source: AEDC Data Dictionary v7.0 (Australian Government Department of Education, February 2025), entry A1d
variable_description: Whether any of the child's absence this school year was never explained to the school. The dictionary describes it as "A variable to identify how many days the child has been absent from school due to un-explained reasons", to the best of the teacher's knowledge. Of the four reason flags this is the one usually read as a risk marker, because it records a gap in contact between the family and the school rather than a stated cause.
value_definition: A single-digit integer, 0 for zero days and 1 for one or more days. The dictionary records that the item was renamed from A4a in 2012.
limitation: It measures what the school was told, not why the child was away, so a family that does not ring in and a family with no reason to keep the child home produce the same value. A single unexplained day sets the flag, which makes it a poor proxy for chronic non-attendance; the total band in A1 is the only volume information on the row.
rationale: The dictionary's A1d entry gives the description, the instrument wording, the two-value code frame and the 2012 rename from A4a, and its sibling entries establish that the four reasons partition explained from unexplained absence.
evidence_quote: A variable to identify how many days the child has been absent from school due to un-explained reasons.
supersedes_rationale: The entry carried 'Unexplained reasons' with the generic no-value-list sentence twice and did not say that the flag turns on a single day.

value_domain: AEDC absence band, original-system five-category form
value_source: AEDC Data Dictionary v7.0 (Australian Government Department of Education, February 2025), entry A1z
variable_description: The same absence question as A1 but on the older, finer response scale that the AEDC dictionary labels the original system. It matters because it is the only column that separates a child with no absence at all from a child with one day: A1 folds both into a single band, while this item keeps 0 days and 1 day apart on a five-point scale. The dictionary gives its instrument text as "How many days has this child been absent since the start of the year" and records it as introduced in 2018, which is why it appears from the 2018 cycle table onwards.
value_definition: A single-digit integer over five categories: 0 for 0 days, 1 for 1 day, 2 for 2 to 5 days, 3 for 6 to 10 days and 4 for greater than 10 days. The dictionary annotates the zero category as new in 2012.
limitation: It cannot support a series back to 2009, because the column is only carried from the 2018 cycle; a trend in zero-absence children has no earlier baseline. Its codes also only partly line up with A1's: 2, 3 and 4 carry the same bands in both, but A1's code 1 covers 0 to 1 day while here code 1 is exactly one day and code 0 holds the children with no absence at all, so pooling the two columns without recoding puts every zero-absence child in the wrong band.
rationale: The dictionary publishes A1z alongside A1 with a different code frame, names it an original-system item in the variable list, and gives 2018 as the cycle in which it was introduced, matching where it appears in the PLIDA tables.
evidence_quote: Variable to indicate how many days the child has been absent from school since the beginning of the school year.
supersedes_rationale: The entry repeated the custodian's 'Original system: how many days has this child been absent since the start of the year' and the generic no-value-list sentence twice, without explaining what 'original system' meant or how the scale differs from A1.

value_source: AEDC Data Dictionary v7.0 (Australian Government Department of Education, February 2025), entry A1az
variable_description: The family or cultural absence question on the older response scale the AEDC dictionary calls the original system, carried alongside the flag version in A1A. Its purpose is given as "To identify, to the best of the teacher's knowledge, how many days the child was absent due to family/cultural obligations, including ceremonies and funerals". The dictionary records it as introduced in 2018, which is why it appears from the 2018 cycle table onwards and not in 2009, 2012 or 2015.
value_definition: A single-digit integer. The dictionary publishes a field format for this item but no code frame, so the categories are not documented; the flag version A1A uses 0 for zero days and 1 for one or more.
limitation: Its categories cannot be assumed to match A1A's, because the dictionary prints no field values for the original-system reason items, so a join or a recode between the two has to be checked against the observed distribution first. Only three of the six cycles carry it, so it cannot anchor a change over the life of the census.
rationale: The dictionary's A1az entry gives the data element description, the purpose, the instrument wording and the 2018 introduction, and prints a field format with no field-value table, which is itself the fact a user needs.
evidence_quote: A variable to identify how many days the child has been absent from school due to family/cultural obligations.
supersedes_rationale: The entry repeated the custodian's long wording as its own description and printed the generic no-value-list sentence as both definition and limitation, without noting that the dictionary genuinely publishes no code frame for this item.

value_source: AEDC Data Dictionary v7.0 (Australian Government Department of Education, February 2025), entry A1bz
variable_description: The illness or injury absence question on the older response scale the AEDC dictionary calls the original system, carried alongside the flag version in A1B. The dictionary describes it as "A variable to identify how many days the child has been absent from school due to illness / injury" and records it as introduced in 2018. It appears only from the 2018 cycle table, so health-related absence before that has to be taken from A1B.

rationale: The dictionary's A1bz entry publishes the description, purpose, instrument wording and 2018 introduction, and shows a field format block with no field-value block.
evidence_quote: A variable to identify how many days the child has been absent from school due to illness / injury.
supersedes_rationale: The entry restated the custodian's wording and printed the generic no-value-list sentence twice, giving no sense of how the original-system item relates to A1B.

value_source: AEDC Data Dictionary v7.0 (Australian Government Department of Education, February 2025), entry A1cz
variable_description: The residual explained-absence question on the older response scale the AEDC dictionary calls the original system, carried alongside the flag version in A1C. The dictionary defines the reason as "other explained reasons", which its 2009 note for the flag version illustrates with climatic and financial circumstances. It was introduced in 2018 and appears only on the 2018, 2021 and 2024 cycle tables.
value_definition: A single-digit integer. No field values are published for this item, so its categories are undocumented; the flag version A1C uses 0 for zero days and 1 for one or more.

rationale: The dictionary's A1cz entry gives the description, purpose, instrument wording and 2018 introduction, and its sibling A1c entry supplies the examples that define the residual category.
evidence_quote: A variable to identify how many days the child has been absent from school due to other explained reasons.
supersedes_rationale: The entry carried the custodian's 'Other explained reasons' with the generic no-value-list sentence as both definition and limitation, and never distinguished the original-system item from A1C.

value_source: AEDC Data Dictionary v7.0 (Australian Government Department of Education, February 2025), entry A1dz
variable_description: The unexplained-absence question on the older response scale the AEDC dictionary calls the original system, carried alongside the flag version in A1D. Like the other original-system reason items it appears only on the 2018, 2021 and 2024 cycle tables, so it covers the last three cycles of the census.
value_definition: A single-digit integer with no field values published in the dictionary. The corresponding flag version A1D is documented as 0 for zero days and 1 for one or more.

rationale: The dictionary's A1dz entry publishes the data element description, the purpose and the instrument wording, and prints a field format block with no field-value block, and the item appears in PLIDA only from the 2018 cycle.

supersedes_rationale: The entry restated 'Unexplained reasons' and printed the generic no-value-list sentence twice, with nothing on how the original-system item differs from A1D or which cycles carry it.

value_domain: AvEDI yes-or-no item (1 yes, 2 no, 88 don't know)
value_source: AEDC Data Dictionary v7.0 (Australian Government Department of Education, February 2025), entry A2
variable_description: Whether the child has turned up to school over- or under-dressed more than once this year, in the teacher's judgement. The instrument asks "Since the start of the year, has the child sometimes (more than once) arrived over or under-dressed for school related activities". It is one of the twelve items, A2 to A13, that the dictionary allocates to the physical health and wellbeing domain, and one of the four (with A3, A4 and A5) that reads as a marker of how well a child arrives ready for the day rather than of motor skill.
value_definition: A two-digit integer coded 1 for yes, 2 for no and 88 for don't know, so a low code is the adverse answer here.
limitation: The coding direction is the opposite of A5, A6, A7 and B10 to B19, which use 1 for no and 2 for yes, so summing raw codes across a section mixes problems with strengths. The item also says nothing about why a child is dressed as they are, and a single occasion does not register at all, since the question sets its threshold at more than once.
rationale: The dictionary's A2 entry gives the description, the instrument text and the three-value code frame, and its section 7.1 table lists A2 among the physical health and wellbeing domain items.
evidence_quote: Since the start of the year, has the child sometimes (more than once) arrived over or under-dressed for school related activities
supersedes_rationale: The entry carried 'Dressed inappropriately' and the generic no-value-list sentence twice, with no code frame, no domain membership and no warning that yes is coded 1 here and 2 elsewhere.

value_domain: AvEDI yes-or-no item (1 yes, 2 no, 88 don't know)
value_source: AEDC Data Dictionary v7.0 (Australian Government Department of Education, February 2025), entry A3
variable_description: Whether the child has arrived too tired or too sick to do schoolwork more than once this year. The instrument combines the two states in one question: "Since the start of the year, has the child sometimes (more than once) arrived too tired and/or too sick to do schoolwork". A3A and A3B split it into tiredness and sickness, but the dictionary records that they are only answered when this item is yes, so this is the gate on both. It counts towards the physical health and wellbeing domain score, which its two follow-ups do not.
value_definition: A two-digit integer coded 1 for yes, 2 for no and 88 for don't know.
limitation: A yes cannot be read as a health signal on its own, because the question fuses fatigue with illness and only the follow-up items separate them; and those follow-ups are missing for New South Wales in the first two cycles. Its threshold of more than once also means an isolated bad morning leaves no trace.
rationale: The dictionary's A3 entry gives the combined instrument wording and the code frame, its A3a and A3b entries record the 'Only answer if A3 = Yes' filter, and section 7.1 lists A3 among the physical health and wellbeing domain items.
evidence_quote: Since the start of the year, has the child sometimes (more than once) arrived too tired and/or too sick to do schoolwork
supersedes_rationale: The entry carried 'Too tired and/or sick' with the generic no-value-list sentence twice, and did not say that this item gates A3A and A3B.

value_domain: AvEDI yes-or-no item (1 yes, 2 no, 88 don't know), filtered
value_source: AEDC Data Dictionary v7.0 (Australian Government Department of Education, February 2025), entry A3a
variable_description: Whether tiredness in particular is behind a yes on A3, asked only of children whose teacher already said they arrived too tired or too sick. The dictionary states the filter plainly as "Only answer if A3 = Yes", and records that the item was "Not provided in New South Wales in Cycle 1/2". Unlike A3 it is not one of the items the dictionary allocates to the physical health and wellbeing domain, so it informs interpretation rather than the score.
value_definition: A two-digit integer coded 1 for yes, 2 for no and 88 for don't know, populated only where A3 is yes.
limitation: A blank does not mean the child is well rested; it usually means the gate question was answered no, or that the child was in New South Wales in 2009 or 2012 when the item was not collected. A national count of tired children taken from this column therefore undercounts, and until the 2015 filter revision the item was asked of all non-NSW students, so the denominator is not the same across cycles.
rationale: The dictionary's A3a entry publishes the instrument wording, the code frame, the New South Wales exclusion for Cycles 1 and 2, and the 2015 filter revision noting the item was previously asked of all non-NSW students.
evidence_quote: Not provided in New South Wales in Cycle 1/2
supersedes_rationale: The entry said only 'Too tired' with the generic no-value-list sentence twice, and never mentioned the conditional filter or the New South Wales gap, which is what makes the column easy to misread.

The instrument wording is "Since the start of the year, has the child sometimes (more than once) arrived too sick to do schoolwork", and the dictionary applies the same "Only answer if A3 = Yes" filter and the same New South Wales exclusion for Cycles 1 and 2 as A3A. A child can be yes on both this item and A3A, so the two do not partition the A3 population.
value_definition: A two-digit integer coded 1 for yes, 2 for no and 88 for don't know, populated only where A3 is yes.

rationale: The dictionary's A3b entry gives the instrument wording, the code frame, the conditional filter, the New South Wales exclusion for Cycles 1 and 2 and the 2015 filter revision.
evidence_quote: Since the start of the year, has the child sometimes (more than once) arrived too sick to do schoolwork
supersedes_rationale: The entry carried 'Too sick' with the generic no-value-list sentence twice, omitting the filter, the jurisdiction gap and the relationship to A3A.

value_domain: AvEDI yes-or-no item (1 yes, 2 no, 88 don't know)
value_source: AEDC Data Dictionary v7.0 (Australian Government Department of Education, February 2025), entry A4
variable_description: Whether the child has arrived at school hungry more than once this year, in the teacher's judgement. The dictionary's purpose is "To identify if, since the start of the year, the child has arrived hungry at school on more than one occasion", and the item counts towards the physical health and wellbeing domain score. A4A on the 2018 and later core tables records whether the child attends a breakfast club, which is the service-side companion to this question.
value_definition: A two-digit integer coded 1 for yes, 2 for no and 88 for don't know.
limitation: It is not a measure of food insecurity: it captures what a teacher noticed in a classroom, so a child fed at a breakfast club before class can be recorded as not hungry while the household situation is unchanged. Because a yes needs more than one occasion, it also cannot flag an acute episode.
rationale: The dictionary's A4 entry gives the description, purpose, instrument wording and code frame, section 7.1 lists A4 among the physical health and wellbeing domain items, and the A4a entry establishes the breakfast club companion item.
evidence_quote: Since the start of the year, has the child sometimes (more than once) arrived hungry
supersedes_rationale: The entry carried 'Hungry' and the generic no-value-list sentence twice, with no code frame and no signal that it is a teacher observation rather than a household measure.

value_domain: AvEDI yes-or-no item with not-applicable (0 no, 1 yes, 88, 99)
value_source: AEDC Data Dictionary v7.0 (Australian Government Department of Education, February 2025), entry A4a
variable_description: Whether the child attends a breakfast club run by the school or the community. The dictionary describes it as a "Variable to indicate if the child attends school/community breakfast club", and it appears in PLIDA only from the 2018 cycle because it was renamed from D12 that year. The 2024 cycle applied "Consistent business rules ... across Cycles to ensure concordance between School Coordinator and Teacher responses for a school", so the answer is reconciled against what the school itself reported from 2015 onwards.
value_definition: A two-digit integer coded 0 for no, 1 for yes, 88 for don't know and 99 for not applicable, the last added in 2015.
limitation: It cannot be read as a child-level exposure to a nutrition programme, because it partly reflects whether the school runs a club at all and has been reconciled to the school coordinator's answer; 99 marks the cases where the question does not arise rather than a child who declined. It is also absent before the 2018 cycle under this name, so a change since 2009 needs the D12 series instead.
rationale: The dictionary's A4a entry publishes the description, instrument wording, four-value code frame, the 2015 addition of code 99, the 2018 rename from D12 and the 2024 concordance rules.
evidence_quote: Consistent business rules applied across Cycles to ensure concordance between School Coordinator and Teacher responses for a school.
supersedes_rationale: The entry carried the custodian's question text as its description and the generic no-value-list sentence twice, with no code frame, no note that 0 rather than 1 is the negative answer, and no mention of the school-level reconciliation.

value_domain: AvEDI yes-or-no item (1 no, 2 yes, 88 don't know)
value_source: AEDC Data Dictionary v7.0 (Australian Government Department of Education, February 2025), entry A5
variable_description: Whether the child can manage the toilet on their own most of the time, in the teacher's judgement. The instrument asks "Would you say this child is independent in toileting habits most of the time", and the dictionary counts the item towards the physical health and wellbeing domain score. It is coded the opposite way round to A2, A3 and A4: here the higher code, 2, is the positive answer.
value_definition: A two-digit integer coded 1 for no, 2 for yes and 88 for don't know, so the direction is reversed relative to the yes-first items earlier in section A.
limitation: It is a judgement about classroom independence, not a clinical statement about continence, and the qualifier 'most of the time' means an occasional accident does not move the answer. The AEDC also does not compute domain categories for children diagnosed with special needs, so this item cannot be used to profile the children for whom toileting support is most likely to be an issue.
rationale: The dictionary's A5 entry gives the description, purpose, instrument wording and the reversed code frame, section 7.1 lists A5 as a physical health and wellbeing item, and section 3.1 states that domain categories are not calculated for children diagnosed with special needs.
evidence_quote: Would you say this child is independent in toileting habits most of the time
supersedes_rationale: The entry said only 'Washroom' and repeated the generic no-value-list sentence, so a reader had neither the question nor the reversed coding, which is where the mistake happens.

value_domain: AvEDI yes-or-no item (1 no, 2 yes, 88 don't know)
value_source: AEDC Data Dictionary v7.0 (Australian Government Department of Education, February 2025), entry A6
variable_description: Whether the child has settled on one hand rather than swapping, in the teacher's judgement. The instrument asks "Would you say this child shows an established hand preference (right vs. left or vice versa)", so the answer is about whether a preference exists, not which hand it is. It is one of the twelve items the dictionary allocates to the physical health and wellbeing domain, where an established preference is treated as a marker of fine motor development.
value_definition: A two-digit integer coded 1 for no, 2 for yes and 88 for don't know.
limitation: It cannot identify left-handed children: both a left-handed and a right-handed child answer yes, and the AvEDI collects no column recording which hand. A no also confounds genuine ambidexterity with a child the teacher has simply not watched closely enough, which is otherwise the 88 category.
rationale: The dictionary's A6 entry gives the instrument wording, which names both hands as equivalent affirmative cases, along with the code frame, and section 7.1 lists A6 as a physical health and wellbeing item.
evidence_quote: Would you say this child shows an established hand preference (right vs. left or vice versa)
supersedes_rationale: The entry said 'Hand preference' with the generic no-value-list sentence twice, which invites the reader to expect a left-or-right code that the column does not carry.

value_domain: AvEDI yes-or-no item (1 no, 2 yes, 88 don't know)
value_source: AEDC Data Dictionary v7.0 (Australian Government Department of Education, February 2025), entry A7
variable_description: Whether the child moves around without bumping into or tripping over things, in the teacher's judgement. The instrument spells the criterion out: "Would you say this child is well co-ordinated (i.e. moves without running into or tripping over things)?". It is the gross motor counterpart to A8 and A9, which rate pen grip and object handling, and all three feed the physical health and wellbeing domain score.
value_definition: A two-digit integer coded 1 for no, 2 for yes and 88 for don't know, in the same direction as A5, A6 and the B-series literacy items.
limitation: It is a single yes-or-no on whole-body movement, so it cannot grade coordination or separate a mild clumsiness from a motor impairment; the three-point items A10 and A12 are the nearest thing to a gradient. A yes also does not mean the child was assessed under comparable conditions, since teachers observe children in very different play spaces.
rationale: The dictionary's A7 entry publishes the instrument wording with its parenthetical criterion and the code frame, and section 7.1 lists A7 among the physical health and wellbeing domain items.
evidence_quote: Would you say this child is well co-ordinated (i.e. moves without running into or tripping over things)?
supersedes_rationale: The entry carried 'Well coordinated' and the generic no-value-list sentence twice, without the criterion the teacher was actually asked to apply.

value_domain: AvEDI three-point proficiency rating (1 poor, 2 average, 3 good, 88 don't know)
value_source: AEDC Data Dictionary v7.0 (Australian Government Department of Education, February 2025), entry A8
variable_description: The teacher's rating of how well the child holds a pen, crayon or brush. The dictionary gives the purpose as "To rate how well the child holds a pen, crayon or brush", and unlike the yes-or-no items earlier in section A this one is graded on three levels. It is a fine motor item in the physical health and wellbeing domain, and the closest physical companion to the writing items B18 to B23 in the language and cognitive domain.
value_definition: A two-digit integer coded 1 for poor or very poor, 2 for average, 3 for very good or good, with 88 for don't know. Both ends of the scale carry a merged label, code 1 covering poor and very poor and code 3 covering good and very good, so the extremes cannot be separated.
limitation: It cannot separate a grip problem from a lack of practice, since a child who has rarely held a pencil and a child with a motor difficulty both rate poor. The merged top and bottom categories also mean the column cannot identify the very poorest or very best writers, which matters if the intent is to find children needing occupational therapy referral.
rationale: The dictionary's A8 entry gives the instrument wording, the purpose and the three-point code frame with its merged end labels and the don't-know convention, and section 7.1 lists A8 as a physical health and wellbeing item.
evidence_quote: How would you rate this child's proficiency at holding a pen, crayon or brush
supersedes_rationale: The entry said 'Proficient at holding pen' with the generic no-value-list sentence twice, so a reader had no idea that the response is a three-point rating with merged extremes.

value_domain: AvEDI three-point proficiency rating (1 poor, 2 average, 3 good, 88 don't know)
value_source: AEDC Data Dictionary v7.0 (Australian Government Department of Education, February 2025), entry A9
variable_description: The teacher's rating of how well the child handles objects, on the same three-point scale as A8, A10, A11, A12 and A13. The instrument asks "How would you rate this child's ability to manipulate objects" without naming particular objects, so the teacher applies it to whatever the classroom offers. It is one of the fine motor items in the physical health and wellbeing domain.
value_definition: A two-digit integer coded 1 for poor or very poor, 2 for average, 3 for very good or good, with 88 for don't know.
limitation: The question names no task, so the rating is anchored to the materials and expectations of one classroom rather than to a fixed standard, which makes it weaker for comparing individual children than for comparing large groups. It also overlaps heavily with A8, so treating the two as independent evidence of fine motor skill double counts one judgement.
rationale: The dictionary's A9 entry publishes the instrument wording, the purpose and the three-point code frame, and section 7.1 lists A9 among the physical health and wellbeing domain items.
evidence_quote: How would you rate this child's ability to manipulate objects
supersedes_rationale: The entry carried 'Manipulates objects' with the generic no-value-list sentence twice and did not say the response is a graded rating.

value_domain: AvEDI three-point proficiency rating (1 poor, 2 average, 3 good, 88 don't know)
value_source: AEDC Data Dictionary v7.0 (Australian Government Department of Education, February 2025), entry A10
variable_description: The teacher's rating of how well the child manages stairs, used in the AvEDI as a gross motor observation. The dictionary gives the purpose as "To rate how well the child can climb stairs" and the instrument text as "How would you rate this child's ability to climb stairs". It sits with A7, A8 and A9 in the physical health and wellbeing domain, and is the only one of them that depends on a particular feature of the school building.
value_definition: A two-digit integer coded 1 for poor or very poor, 2 for average, 3 for very good or good, with 88 for don't know.
limitation: A don't-know answer here often means the school is single storey rather than that the child is unobserved, so the missing pattern is a property of the building and can correlate with remoteness and school size. The item also cannot detect a mobility aid or a physical disability; the D-series items in the AEDC special needs table carry that.
rationale: The dictionary's A10 entry gives the description, purpose, instrument wording and three-point code frame, section 5.2 sets 88 as the don't-know convention for all AvEDI items, and section 7.1 lists A10 as a physical health and wellbeing item.
evidence_quote: How would you rate this child's ability to climb stairs
supersedes_rationale: The entry said 'Climbs stairs' and printed the generic no-value-list sentence twice, with nothing on the rating scale or on why the item is missing so often.

value_domain: AvEDI three-point proficiency rating (1 poor, 2 average, 3 good, 88 don't know)
value_source: AEDC Data Dictionary v7.0 (Australian Government Department of Education, February 2025), entry A11
variable_description: The teacher's rating of how much energy the child sustains across the school day. The instrument asks "How would you rate this child's level of energy throughout the school day", which makes it a judgement about stamina over a whole day rather than about activity at one moment. It counts towards the physical health and wellbeing domain score and is the graded companion to A3, which asks only whether the child has arrived too tired or sick.
value_definition: A two-digit integer coded 1 for poor or very poor, 2 for average, 3 for very good or good, with 88 for don't know.
limitation: High energy is scored as good, so the scale rewards a child who is lively and penalises a quiet or withdrawn one, which means the column cannot be read as an inattention or hyperactivity measure; the EMOT_4 sub-domain, hyperactive and inattentive behaviour, covers that. It also gives no clue whether low energy comes from sleep, nutrition, illness or a long journey to school.
rationale: The dictionary's A11 entry gives the instrument wording and the three-point code frame, and section 7.1 lists A11 among the physical health and wellbeing domain items, distinct from the emotional maturity items in section C.
evidence_quote: How would you rate this child's level of energy throughout the school day
supersedes_rationale: The entry carried 'Level of energy' with the generic no-value-list sentence twice, and gave no direction to the scale, which matters because low is the adverse end here.

value_domain: AvEDI three-point proficiency rating (1 poor, 2 average, 3 good, 88 don't know)
value_source: AEDC Data Dictionary v7.0 (Australian Government Department of Education, February 2025), entry A12
variable_description: The teacher's overall impression of the child's physical development, asked as a single summary judgement rather than a specific skill. The dictionary gives the purpose as "To rate the child's overall physical development", and the item enters the physical health and wellbeing domain score alongside the eleven specific items A2 to A11 and A13. It is the only item in section A that asks the teacher to generalise.
value_definition: A two-digit integer coded 1 for poor or very poor, 2 for average, 3 for very good or good, with 88 for don't know.
limitation: It is not a substitute for the PHYS domain score, even though both summarise the same territory: PHYS is calculated from the whole item set under a licensed methodology, while this is one teacher's global impression scored on three levels. Nothing physical is measured behind it, so it carries no height, weight or health information.
rationale: The dictionary's A12 entry gives the purpose and the three-point code frame, section 3.1 states that domain scores are calculated by combining the specific domain items under a methodology licensed from the Offord Centre, and section 7.1 lists A12 among those items.
evidence_quote: How would you rate this child's overall physical development
supersedes_rationale: The entry carried 'Overall physical' and the generic no-value-list sentence twice, and left open the misreading that this column is the physical domain score.

value_domain: AvEDI three-point proficiency rating (1 poor, 2 average, 3 good, 88 don't know)
value_source: AEDC Data Dictionary v7.0 (Australian Government Department of Education, February 2025), entry A13
variable_description: The teacher's rating of the child's day-to-day personal hygiene, on the same three-point scale as A8 to A12. It is the last of the twelve items the dictionary allocates to the physical health and wellbeing domain, and pairs with A5 on toileting and A2 on dress as the items about how a child arrives and looks after themselves rather than about motor skill. The instrument asks simply "How would you rate this child's daily personal hygiene".
value_definition: A two-digit integer coded 1 for poor or very poor, 2 for average, 3 for very good or good, with 88 for don't know.
limitation: It is a teacher's assessment against an unstated standard, so it can track household resources, cultural expectations or the teacher's own norms as readily as the child's development, and the AEDC publishes no guidance on where the boundary between average and poor sits. It is not evidence of neglect and should not be used as a proxy for one.
rationale: The dictionary's A13 entry gives the description, purpose, instrument wording and three-point code frame, and section 7.1 lists A13 among the physical health and wellbeing domain items.
evidence_quote: How would you rate this child's daily personal hygiene
supersedes_rationale: The entry said 'Daily personal hygiene' with the generic no-value-list sentence twice, and gave no scale and no warning about how subjective the judgement is.

value_source: AEDC Data Dictionary v7.0 (Australian Government Department of Education, February 2025), entry AGCampusID
variable_description: The Commonwealth's own code for the school campus at which the child was assessed. The dictionary defines it as "The individual campus code used by the Australian Government to identify each school campus participating in the AEDC", held on the Master Unit Record File and "Suppressed for schools outside of a data recipient's jurisdiction". It appears in PLIDA only on the 2018 cycle table, because the dictionary records the item being replaced by AGLocationID from 2021 and fully discontinued in 2024.
value_definition: A five-digit integer allocated by the Australian Government, not a serial within the AEDC file, so the value range is set by the national school register rather than by this collection.
limitation: It cannot follow a school across cycles in PLIDA, since only the 2018 table carries it and its successors sit under different names; SCHOOLID is the identifier present in every cycle. It also identifies a campus, not a school or a teacher, so a multi-campus school splits across values while TEACHERID separates classes within a campus.
rationale: The dictionary's AGCampusID entry gives the definition, the five-digit format, the Master URF availability, the jurisdictional suppression rule and the 2021 replacement and 2024 discontinuation, which together explain why it appears in one PLIDA cycle only.
evidence_quote: The individual campus code used by the Australian Government to identify each school campus participating in the AEDC.
supersedes_rationale: The entry carried the custodian's 'National campus identifier used by deewr' with the generic no-value-list sentence twice, and gave no hint that the identifier is suppressed outside a recipient's jurisdiction or that it lives on only one cycle.

value_source: AEDC Data Dictionary v7.0 (Australian Government Department of Education, February 2025), entry AgeCat
variable_description: The finest published banding of the child's age, in steps of roughly three months across the school-entry range. It is a derived variable, built from the age the dictionary describes as "based on the student's reported date of birth and the date on which the Instrument was completed by the teacher". AGECUT, AGEGROUP and AGEGROUP3TO7 on the same row are coarser cuts of the same underlying age, and AGEINMONTHS is the ungrouped version.
value_definition: A two-digit integer from 0 to 15, so sixteen codes despite the name; the '15 narrow' in the custodian's label counts the non-zero codes. Codes 1 to 13 step in roughly three-month intervals from 3 years 8 months to 6 years 10 months; code 0 is everything under 3 years 8 months, code 14 spans 6 years 10 months to 7 years 6 months, and code 15 is everything above.
limitation: The bands are not equal width, so treating the code as a linear age scale compresses the middle and stretches both tails, and a regression on the raw code will not recover a per-month effect. Age is also measured at the day the teacher completed the instrument rather than at a fixed census date, so two children on the same code were assessed at different points in the school year.
rationale: The dictionary's AgeCat entry publishes all sixteen bands with their exact year-and-month boundaries and marks the variable as derived, and section 4.4 states how AEDC age is constructed.
evidence_quote: AEDC age is based on the student's reported date of birth and the date on which the Instrument was completed by the teacher.
supersedes_rationale: The entry said only 'Age categories (15 narrow)' with the generic no-value-list sentence twice, giving neither the number of codes nor the fact that the bands are uneven at both ends.

value_source: AEDC Data Dictionary v7.0 (Australian Government Department of Education, February 2025), entry AgeCut
variable_description: The coarsest numeric grouping of the child's age, splitting the cohort into under five, five, and six or older. The dictionary marks it as derived and gives its purpose as "A grouping variable for child age", which is what it is normally used for: a control or a cross-tabulation axis when the sixteen bands of AGECAT are too fine. AGEGROUP holds the same idea as text with the top group cut at seven rather than six.
value_definition: A single-digit integer with three codes: 0 for under 5 years, 1 for 5 years and 2 for 6 years and older.
limitation: Its top and bottom categories are open, so a four-year-old and a three-year-old share code 0 while a six-year-old and an eight-year-old share code 2, which hides exactly the age spread that matters when comparing schools with different entry rules. The bottom category also mixes children the AEDC excludes from domain categories, those under four years, with four-year-olds who are scored.
rationale: The dictionary's AgeCut entry gives the purpose, the derived source and the three-code frame, and section 3.1 records that domain categories are not calculated for children less than four years of age.
evidence_quote: Domain indicator categories are not calculated for children diagnosed with special needs, or children less than four years of age.
supersedes_rationale: The entry carried 'Age categories (3 broad)' and the generic no-value-list sentence twice, without the cut points or the interaction with the under-four exclusion.

value_source: AEDC Data Dictionary v7.0 (Australian Government Department of Education, February 2025), entry AgeGroup
variable_description: The confidentialised age grouping the AEDC uses in its published outputs, held as text rather than as a code. Section 4.4 of the dictionary says the age variable is "available in years and is confidentialised as follows" and then lists under five years, five years, six years and over six years, and this is the column that carries that grouping. AGECUT expresses almost the same split numerically, but its top band starts at six while this one holds six-year-olds separately and reserves its top value for seven and over.
value_definition: A two-character text field with four values: '<5' for under 5 years, '5' for 5 to under 6, '6' for 6 to under 7, and '>6' for 7 years and over. The field is left justified, not numeric.
limitation: Two of its four values are not numbers, so converting the column to numeric silently drops the youngest and oldest children to missing and leaves an apparently clean five-and-six-year-old sample that is missing its tails. The label '>6' is also misleading on its own, since the dictionary defines it as age 7 years or more rather than anything above six.
rationale: The dictionary's AgeGroup entry gives the four text values with their exact age boundaries and records the field as text with left justification, and section 4.4 states the confidentialisation rule the grouping implements.
evidence_quote: This variable is available in years and is confidentialised as follows:
supersedes_rationale: The entry said only 'Age group' with the generic no-value-list sentence twice, and did not warn that the column is text or that '>6' means seven and over.

value_domain: AEDC age in completed years, top coded at 7
value_source: AEDC Data Dictionary v7.0 (Australian Government Department of Education, February 2025), entry AgeGroup3to7
variable_description: The child's age in completed years at the time the teacher filled in the instrument, held as a plain integer from 3 to 7. It is the numeric age variable most convenient for analysis on the AEDC core tables, and the dictionary marks it as derived rather than reported. AGEINMONTHS is the finer version of the same quantity, AGECAT the finer banding, and AGEGROUP the text grouping used for publication.
value_definition: A single-digit integer taking 3 for age 3 to under 4, 4 for 4 to under 5, 5 for 5 to under 6, 6 for 6 to under 7, and 7 for 7 and over. Only the top code is open; the others are exact one-year intervals.
limitation: Its name suggests a range of three to seven, but code 7 is a top code with no upper bound, so an eight-year-old repeating a year is indistinguishable from a child who has just turned seven. Rounding down to completed years also loses up to eleven months of development, which is large relative to the age effects the AEDC domain cut-offs are designed to absorb.
rationale: The dictionary's AgeGroup3to7 entry publishes the five codes with their exact age intervals and marks the source as derived, and section 4.4 states that AEDC age is built from date of birth against the instrument completion date.
evidence_quote: Age >= 7
supersedes_rationale: The entry carried the custodian's 'Age in years' with the generic no-value-list sentence twice, so it never said that 7 is a top code rather than an exact age.

value_source: AEDC Data Dictionary v7.0 (Australian Government Department of Education, February 2025), entry AgeInMonths
variable_description: The child's age in whole months when the teacher completed the instrument, and the finest age measure on the AEDC file. The dictionary marks it as derived and section 4.4 explains the derivation: "AEDC age is based on the student's reported date of birth and the date on which the Instrument was completed by the teacher." Every other age column on the row, AGECAT, AGECUT, AGEGROUP and AGEGROUP3TO7, is a banding of this quantity.
value_definition: A three-digit integer counting completed months, so a child of five years and three months is 63. There is no code frame; the domain is open across the school-entry age range.
limitation: It is age at assessment, not age at a common reference date, so it moves with when in the school year the teacher happened to complete the instrument as much as with the child's date of birth; MOC, the month of completion, is the column needed to adjust for that. It also cannot be turned back into a date of birth, which is not released.
rationale: The dictionary's AgeInMonths entry gives the derived source and the three-digit integer format, and section 4.4 states the derivation from reported date of birth against the instrument completion date.
evidence_quote: AEDC age is based on the student's reported date of birth and the date on which the Instrument was completed by the teacher.
supersedes_rationale: The entry restated 'Age in months' and printed the generic no-value-list sentence twice, without saying what the age is measured against, which is the whole difficulty with the column.

value_domain: Year of first arrival in Australia (four-digit year, 9999 unknown)
value_source: AEDC Data Dictionary v7.0 (Australian Government Department of Education, February 2025), entry ArrivalYear
variable_description: The year the child first came to Australia, asked on the instrument as "In which year did the child first arrive in Australia". Read against AGEINMONTHS it gives an approximate age at migration, and against COUNTRY and PLACEOFBIRTH on the same row it distinguishes a child born overseas who arrived as an infant from one who arrived shortly before starting school. The dictionary records the item as introduced in 2015, which is why it is absent from the 2009 and 2012 cycle tables.
value_definition: A four-digit integer holding a calendar year, with 9999 reserved for unknown. There is no separate not-applicable code for children born in Australia.
limitation: The 9999 sentinel is a valid four-digit year to any arithmetic, so a mean or a difference computed without excluding it is badly wrong. It also records the first arrival, so a child who left and returned is dated by the earlier trip, and it says nothing about visa status or whether the family arrived together.
rationale: The dictionary's ArrivalYear entry gives the definition, the instrument wording, the four-digit format with 9999 for unknown, and the 2015 introduction, matching the cycles on which the column appears in PLIDA.
evidence_quote: In which year did the child first arrive in Australia
supersedes_rationale: The entry said 'Year of arrival' with the generic no-value-list sentence twice, and did not disclose the 9999 sentinel, which is the practical trap in the column.

value_domain: Indigenous status (Aboriginal and/or Torres Strait Islander origin)
value_source: AEDC Data Dictionary v7.0 (Australian Government Department of Education, February 2025), entry ATSI
variable_description: Whether the child is recorded as being of Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander origin, the gate on every other item in the AEDC Indigenous table. The dictionary defines it as follows: "A child is considered to be 'Indigenous' if he or she identifies as being of Aboriginal and/or Torres Strait Islander origin. The term 'origin' is considered to relate to people's Australian Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander descent and for some, but not all, their cultural identity." ATSITYPE beside it splits Aboriginal from Torres Strait Islander origin, and B1A to B1D rate the child's use of Aboriginal English, Kriol and traditional languages.
value_definition: A single-digit integer, documented by the AEDC as 0 for no and 1 for yes. The PLIDA data item list describes the field differently, as 1 for Indigenous with null signifying non-Indigenous or non-identifying, so the negative case may arrive as missing rather than as zero.
limitation: The two published descriptions disagree on how a non-Indigenous child is stored, so a test written as ATSI equals 0 can return nobody while ATSI equals 1 works; check the observed values before building a denominator. The item is also a school enrolment record of origin rather than a self-report by the child or family at census time, and 'not identifying' is indistinguishable from 'not Indigenous' in either coding.
rationale: The dictionary's ATSI entry carries the full origin definition, the instrument wording and the two-value code frame, and the PLIDA data item list for the same column states a different missing convention, which is the discrepancy a user has to resolve.
evidence_quote: A child is considered to be 'Indigenous' if he or she identifies as being of Aboriginal and/or Torres Strait Islander origin.
supersedes_rationale: The entry carried only the PLIDA wording about nulls and repeated the generic no-value-list sentence twice, without the AEDC's own definition of origin or any note that the two sources describe the coding differently.

value_domain: Indigenous origin type (Aboriginal, Torres Strait Islander, both, neither, not stated)
value_source: AEDC Data Dictionary v7.0 (Australian Government Department of Education, February 2025), entry ATSIType
variable_description: Which Indigenous origin the child is recorded as having, asked only where ATSI on the same row is yes. The dictionary states the filter as "Only answer if ATSI = Yes" and the jurisdictional rule as "Not provided in New South Wales", with a 2015 filter revision noting that previous cycles did not include NSW students at all. Its purpose is to add detail rather than to change the count of Indigenous children, which ATSI alone establishes.
value_definition: A single-digit integer with five codes: 1 Aboriginal but not Torres Strait Islander origin, 2 Torres Strait Islander but not Aboriginal origin, 3 both, 4 neither, and 9 not stated or unknown. The 2012 cycle revised these field values.
limitation: Its blanks are dominated by the filter and by New South Wales, so a national split of Aboriginal against Torres Strait Islander children taken from this column omits the largest jurisdiction and is not comparable across cycles. Code 4, neither origin, can also appear on rows where ATSI is yes, so the two columns can contradict each other and ATSI should be the one used to define the population.
rationale: The dictionary's ATSIType entry gives the purpose, the instrument wording, the five-code frame, the conditional filter on ATSI, the New South Wales exclusion and the 2012 and 2015 revisions.
evidence_quote: Only answer if ATSI = Yes
supersedes_rationale: The entry said 'Indigenous background' with the generic no-value-list sentence twice, and never disclosed the filter, the New South Wales gap or the internally contradictory 'neither' code.

value_domain: AvEDI three-point proficiency rating with not-applicable (1 poor, 2 average, 3 good, 88, 99)
value_source: AEDC Data Dictionary v7.0 (Australian Government Department of Education, February 2025), entry B1
variable_description: The teacher's rating of how effectively the child uses English, asked as "How would you rate this child's ability to use language effectively in English". The dictionary allocates it to the communication skills and general knowledge domain, not to language and cognitive skills, so it feeds COMGEN rather than LANGCOG. B1A to B1D in the AEDC Indigenous table carry the parallel ratings for Aboriginal English, Kriol, traditional languages and other Indigenous languages, and ESL and LANG on the core table record whether English is the home language at all.
value_definition: A two-digit integer coded 1 for poor or very poor, 2 for average, 3 for very good or good, with 88 for don't know and 99 for not applicable. It is one of the few AvEDI items to carry the not-applicable code.
limitation: A low rating is not evidence of a language delay: the item rates English specifically, so a child fluent in another language and new to English scores at the bottom on linguistic competence they in fact have. Reading it alongside LBOTE, ESL and the B1A to B1D Indigenous language ratings is the only way to tell the two situations apart.
rationale: The dictionary's B1 entry gives the instrument wording and the five-value code frame, section 7.1 lists B1 under the communication skills and general knowledge domain, and the B1a entry establishes the parallel other-language items.
evidence_quote: How would you rate this child's ability to use language effectively in English
supersedes_rationale: The entry carried 'Proficient in english' with the generic no-value-list sentence twice, and did not say which domain the item feeds or that a low score can reflect language background rather than ability.

value_domain: AvEDI yes-or-no item (1 no, 2 yes, 88 don't know)
value_source: AEDC Data Dictionary v7.0 (Australian Government Department of Education, February 2025), entry B10
variable_description: Whether the child shows curiosity about printed material, asked as "Would you say this child is interested in reading (inquisitive/curious about the meaning of printed material)?". It is one of the twenty-six items, B8 to B33, that the dictionary allocates to the language and cognitive skills domain, and it sits at the disposition end of that set: B11 to B17 test what the child can actually do with letters and words. E7 on the core table records whether the child is read to at home.
value_definition: A two-digit integer coded 1 for no, 2 for yes and 88 for don't know, so the higher code is the positive answer across the whole B10 to B19 block.
limitation: It rates an attitude the teacher infers from behaviour in class, so a child who is interested in books at home but reticent at school reads as a no; it is not a measure of reading ability, which B15 to B17 carry. The binary form also gives no gradient, so it cannot separate mild from strong interest.
rationale: The dictionary's B10 entry gives the instrument wording with its parenthetical criterion and the code frame, and section 7.1 lists B10 among the language and cognitive skills domain items.
evidence_quote: Would you say this child is interested in reading (inquisitive/curious about the meaning of printed material)?
supersedes_rationale: The entry carried 'Interested in reading' with the generic no-value-list sentence twice, giving neither the code direction nor the distinction from the reading skill items.

value_domain: AvEDI yes-or-no item (1 no, 2 yes, 88 don't know)
value_source: AEDC Data Dictionary v7.0 (Australian Government Department of Education, February 2025), entry B11
variable_description: Whether the child can name at least some letters of the alphabet, the first rung of the literacy ladder in the AvEDI. The instrument asks "Would you say this child is able to identify some letters of the alphabet", with no threshold on how many. It is a language and cognitive skills domain item and the base for B12, which asks whether the child can attach sounds to letters.
value_definition: A two-digit integer coded 1 for no, 2 for yes and 88 for don't know.
limitation: Because 'some' is undefined, the item saturates: most children in their first year of school answer yes, so it separates the very lowest group from everyone else and carries almost no information about the rest. It also does not distinguish recognising a letter shape from knowing its name or its sound.
rationale: The dictionary's B11 entry gives the instrument wording, which sets the threshold at 'some letters', along with the code frame, and section 7.1 lists B11 among the language and cognitive skills domain items.
evidence_quote: Would you say this child is able to identify some letters of the alphabet
supersedes_rationale: The entry said 'Identifies letters' with the generic no-value-list sentence twice, and did not convey how low the threshold is.

value_domain: AvEDI yes-or-no item (1 no, 2 yes, 88 don't know)
value_source: AEDC Data Dictionary v7.0 (Australian Government Department of Education, February 2025), entry B12
variable_description: Whether the child can attach sounds to letters, the phonics step between recognising letters in B11 and reading words in B15. The dictionary gives its purpose as "To identify if the child is able to attach sounds to letters", asked of the teacher as a single yes-or-no judgement. It is one of the language and cognitive skills domain items and, with B13 on rhyming, one of the two phonological awareness questions in the instrument.
value_definition: A two-digit integer coded 1 for no, 2 for yes and 88 for don't know.
limitation: It is the teacher's impression from ordinary classroom work rather than a phonics assessment, so it will track how much explicit phonics teaching the class has done as well as the child's own skill. Nothing in the column says how many letter-sound correspondences the child knows, so it cannot be used to rank children within the yes group.
rationale: The dictionary's B12 entry gives the data element description, the purpose, the instrument wording and the code frame, and section 7.1 lists B12 among the language and cognitive skills domain items.
evidence_quote: Would you say this child is able to attach sounds to letters
supersedes_rationale: The entry carried 'Sounds to letters' and the generic no-value-list sentence twice, with no code frame and no placement in the literacy sequence.

value_domain: AvEDI yes-or-no item (1 no, 2 yes, 88 don't know)
value_source: AEDC Data Dictionary v7.0 (Australian Government Department of Education, February 2025), entry B13
variable_description: Whether the child notices that words rhyme, asked as "Would you say this child is showing awareness of rhyming words". Rhyme awareness is the oral side of early literacy, so this item and B12 on letter sounds are the two phonological questions in a block otherwise concerned with print. It counts towards the language and cognitive skills domain score.
value_definition: A two-digit integer coded 1 for no, 2 for yes and 88 for don't know.
limitation: Rhyme is language specific, so a child whose home language is not English can show the awareness in that language and still be rated no here, which is why B1, LBOTE and ESL belong in any interpretation of a low score. The wording asks only whether awareness is showing, not whether the child can produce rhymes, so a yes sets a low bar.
rationale: The dictionary's B13 entry gives the description, purpose, instrument wording and code frame, and section 7.1 lists B13 among the language and cognitive skills domain items alongside the print-based items.
evidence_quote: Would you say this child is showing awareness of rhyming words
supersedes_rationale: The entry said 'Rhyming awareness' with the generic no-value-list sentence twice, and gave no sense of how the item behaves for children who speak another language at home.

value_domain: AvEDI yes-or-no item (1 no, 2 yes, 88 don't know)
value_source: AEDC Data Dictionary v7.0 (Australian Government Department of Education, February 2025), entry B14
variable_description: Whether the child can take part in group reading activities, the only item in the literacy block that is about behaviour in a group rather than an individual skill. The dictionary's purpose is "To identify if the child is able to participate in group reading activities". It counts towards the language and cognitive skills domain, but what it measures overlaps with the classroom conduct items in section C, since sitting through a shared book requires attention as much as reading.
value_definition: A two-digit integer coded 1 for no, 2 for yes and 88 for don't know.
limitation: It depends on the classroom running group reading at all, so a no can mean the activity does not happen rather than that the child cannot join in, and the don't-know code is the only place that shows. It also confounds reading with attention and social participation, so it should not be read as evidence about reading skill on its own.
rationale: The dictionary's B14 entry gives the description, purpose, instrument wording and code frame, and section 7.1 places B14 in the language and cognitive skills domain while the attention and conduct items sit in the social competence and emotional maturity domains.
evidence_quote: Would you say this child is able to participate in group reading activities
supersedes_rationale: The entry carried 'Group reading' with the generic no-value-list sentence twice, and did not flag that the item is conditional on classroom practice.

value_domain: AvEDI yes-or-no item (1 no, 2 yes, 88 don't know)
value_source: AEDC Data Dictionary v7.0 (Australian Government Department of Education, February 2025), entry B15
variable_description: Whether the child can read simple words, the first of three items that step up in difficulty through B16 for complex words and B17 for simple sentences. The instrument asks "Would you say this child is able to read simple words", leaving 'simple' to the teacher's judgement. All three are language and cognitive skills domain items, and together they are the part of the AvEDI that discriminates among the more advanced readers at school entry.
value_definition: A two-digit integer coded 1 for no, 2 for yes and 88 for don't know.
limitation: The instrument does not enforce the ladder, so a child can be coded no here and yes on B16 or B17; the three items are not a scale and should not be summed without checking for those inconsistent patterns. What counts as a simple word is also left to the teacher, so the threshold moves between classrooms.
rationale: The dictionary's B15, B16 and B17 entries give three separate items of increasing difficulty with identical code frames and no stated filter between them, and section 7.1 lists all three among the language and cognitive skills domain items.
evidence_quote: Would you say this child is able to read simple words
supersedes_rationale: The entry said 'Reads simple words' with the generic no-value-list sentence twice, and gave no warning that the reading items are not a validated ordered scale.

value_domain: AvEDI yes-or-no item (1 no, 2 yes, 88 don't know)
value_source: AEDC Data Dictionary v7.0 (Australian Government Department of Education, February 2025), entry B16
variable_description: Whether the child can read complex words, the middle rung between simple words in B15 and simple sentences in B17. The dictionary's purpose statement is "To identify if the child is able to read complex words", with no definition of complexity offered to the teacher. It is a language and cognitive skills domain item and, being a yes for only a minority of children at school entry, one of the items that does most to separate advanced readers.
value_definition: A two-digit integer coded 1 for no, 2 for yes and 88 for don't know.
limitation: Complexity is undefined in the instrument, so the teacher supplies the standard and the item cannot be benchmarked against any external reading level or against NAPLAN later on. Because few children score yes, small changes in teacher interpretation move the national rate more than they would for a common item like B11.
rationale: The dictionary's B16 entry gives the description, purpose, instrument wording and code frame, and section 7.1 lists B16 among the language and cognitive skills domain items between B15 and B17.
evidence_quote: Would you say this child is able to read complex words
supersedes_rationale: The entry carried 'Reads complex words' with the generic no-value-list sentence twice, and did not say that the standard for 'complex' is left to the teacher.

value_domain: AvEDI yes-or-no item (1 no, 2 yes, 88 don't know)
value_source: AEDC Data Dictionary v7.0 (Australian Government Department of Education, February 2025), entry B17
variable_description: Whether the child can read simple sentences, the top of the three reading items in the AvEDI. The dictionary's data element description reads "Variable to indicate if the child reads sentences", with the instrument asking specifically about simple sentences. A yes marks a child already reading connected text in their first year of school, which is why this item and B16 carry most of the weight at the strong end of the language and cognitive skills domain.
value_definition: A two-digit integer coded 1 for no, 2 for yes and 88 for don't know.
limitation: It records decoding, not comprehension: the question asks whether the child can read the sentence, not whether they understood it, and no item in the instrument covers understanding of connected text. A no is also the normal answer for children starting school, so it should not be treated as a difficulty marker on its own.
rationale: The dictionary's B17 entry gives the data element description, the purpose, the instrument wording and the code frame, and section 7.1 lists B17 among the language and cognitive skills domain items.
evidence_quote: Would you say this child is able to read simple sentences
supersedes_rationale: The entry said 'Reads sentences' with the generic no-value-list sentence twice, and left the reader unable to tell whether the item covers comprehension.

value_domain: AvEDI yes-or-no item (1 no, 2 yes, 88 don't know)
value_source: AEDC Data Dictionary v7.0 (Australian Government Department of Education, February 2025), entry B18
variable_description: Whether the child plays with writing tools, the first of the writing items that run through to B23. The dictionary's purpose is "To identify if the child is experimenting with writing tools", so the criterion is willingness to try rather than any product. It counts towards the language and cognitive skills domain, and the physical companion is A8, which rates how well the child actually holds a pen, crayon or brush.
value_definition: A two-digit integer coded 1 for no, 2 for yes and 88 for don't know.
limitation: Experimenting with a pencil is not writing, so a yes says nothing about whether the child can form letters, which B21 to B23 ask. Access matters too: a classroom or home with few materials suppresses the behaviour without any difference in the child's development.
rationale: The dictionary's B18 entry gives the description, purpose, instrument wording and code frame, and section 7.1 lists B18 with B19 to B23 among the language and cognitive skills domain items.
evidence_quote: Would you say this child is experimenting with writing tools
supersedes_rationale: The entry carried 'Experiments writing' with the generic no-value-list sentence twice, and did not distinguish willingness to try from writing ability.

value_domain: AvEDI yes-or-no item (1 no, 2 yes, 88 don't know)
value_source: AEDC Data Dictionary v7.0 (Australian Government Department of Education, February 2025), entry B19
variable_description: Whether the child knows which way English is written on a page, asked as "Would you say this child is aware of writing directions in English (left to right, top to bottom)". It is a concepts-of-print item rather than a writing skill: it tests orientation, which typically precedes forming letters in B21 to B23. It counts towards the language and cognitive skills domain score.
value_definition: A two-digit integer coded 1 for no, 2 for yes and 88 for don't know.
limitation: The item is tied to English orthography, so a child already literate in a right-to-left or vertically written script is recorded as unaware of writing direction when in fact they hold a different convention; nothing in the AvEDI records that. It also tests knowledge of the page, not handwriting, so a yes carries no information about legibility.
rationale: The dictionary's B19 entry gives the description, purpose and instrument wording, which name English and the left-to-right, top-to-bottom sequence explicitly, along with the code frame, and section 7.1 lists B19 among the language and cognitive skills domain items.
evidence_quote: Would you say this child is aware of writing directions in English (left to right, top to bottom)
supersedes_rationale: The entry said 'Writing directions' with the generic no-value-list sentence twice, and omitted that the item is specific to English writing convention.

value_source: Australian Early Development Census Data Dictionary, version 5.0 (March 2019), Australian Government Department of Education and Training
variable_description: A teacher's rating of how well the child uses Aboriginal English in the classroom or playground, asked as one of four language options under item B1. The data dictionary gives the instrument wording as "How would you rate this child's ability to use languages other than Standard Australian English effectively in the classroom / playground: Aboriginal English (AE)". It sits in aedc_2009_ind beside ATSI, ATSITYPE and the Indigenous language identifiers, and from the 2015 cycle it is only asked when ATSITYPE records the child as Aboriginal, Torres Strait Islander or both; in earlier cycles it was asked of every student outside New South Wales.
value_definition: A single integer on the AvEDI rating scale: 1 poor or very poor, 2 average, 3 very good or good. The AEDC-wide missing conventions apply on top of that, so 88 is don't know and 99 is not applicable.
limitation: It rates a teacher's judgement of ability, not whether the child actually speaks Aboriginal English, and a teacher who does not speak the variety may record 88 rather than a low score. A blank cannot be read as 'no ability' either, because the item was never fielded in New South Wales in cycles 1 and 2 and is filtered on Indigenous status from 2015. It also feeds no domain score: only B1 counts towards communication skills and general knowledge.
rationale: The data dictionary devotes a page to B1a giving the instrument text, the code list, the Indigenous-status filter and the 2015 filter revision, none of which the registry label carried.
evidence_quote: How would you rate this child's ability to use languages other than Standard Australian English effectively in the classroom / playground: Aboriginal English (AE)
supersedes_rationale: The entry carried the custodian's label 'Aboriginal English (AE)' with the generic sentence 'The source metadata does not publish a finite value list.' printed as both the value definition and the limitation, so it never said the field is a rating, who was asked, or that whole jurisdictions are absent.

variable_description: Whether a child who never completes work on time could complete it if given additional time, asked only as a follow-up. The Australian Government licences the method that turns these items into a domain score from the Offord Centre for Child Studies, so the item weights are not public.
value_definition: One integer on the AEDC's three-point frequency scale, ordered the opposite way to the positively worded items: 1 is Often or very true, 2 is Sometimes or somewhat true and 3 is Never or not true. The item describes a problem behaviour, so the reversal keeps 3 as the favourable answer right across the instrument. Don't know is coded 88 and not applicable 99.
